JAMA Dermatology

Estrogen Use and Porphyria Cutanea Tarda

Erichsen PA, Heerfordt IM, Mogensen M et al. · 2026 Oct 28
Study Type: Nationwide matched case-control study (Danish registries, 1995–2024)
Key Question: Is estrogen-containing therapy associated with incident porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT), and does this vary by therapy type or route of administration?
Key Findings:
  • Any estrogen exposure within 1 year before diagnosis was more common in cases (35.2%) than controls (21.5%): adjusted OR 2.03 (95% CI 1.66–2.49; 438 cases, 43,800 controls).
  • Associations were seen for estrogen-containing contraceptives (aOR 2.52; 1.67–3.82), combined estrogen-progestogen therapy (aOR 2.18; 1.53–3.11), and estrogen-only therapy (aOR 1.58; 1.23–2.03).
  • Oral estrogen was associated with PCT (aOR 2.44; 1.66–3.59); nonoral routes were not.
Clinical Relevance: Supports considering oral estrogen as a modifiable risk factor when assessing women with PCT, and suggests nonoral routes may be preferable where estrogen therapy is needed in patients with, or at risk of, PCT.
Limitations: Prescription redemption is a proxy for actual use, and PCT diagnosis relied on hospital coding without biochemical confirmation, with possible residual confounding (e.g. HFE status, hepatitis C) and limited power for nonoral subgroups.

British Journal of Dermatology

Phenome-wide Longitudinal Association Study of Hospital-recorded Comorbidity in Psoriasis

Leonard G, Emdin A, McSweeney SM et al. · 2026 Oct 30
Study Type: Matched cohort study (phenome-wide association design) using linked UK primary and secondary care data (CPRD Aurum–HES).
Key Question: Which hospital-recorded comorbidities are associated with psoriasis across the full spectrum of ICD-10-CM disease categories?
Key Findings:
  • 320,220 adults with psoriasis were compared with 1,706,424 matched controls across 225 ICD blocks; associations spanned multiple organ systems.
  • Long-term associations: liver disease (HR 1.47, 99% CI 1.42–1.51), substance misuse including alcohol and tobacco (HR 1.26, 1.25–1.28; RD 3.27), and interstitial respiratory disease (HR 1.33, 1.27–1.40).
  • Models were adjusted for alcohol, smoking, BMI and deprivation.
Clinical Relevance: In a UK population, the findings support attention to liver and respiratory comorbidity, and to alcohol and tobacco use, alongside established screening, which may inform pre-treatment assessment and monitoring.
Limitations: Hypothesis-generating design with multiple comparisons, and residual confounding (e.g. alcohol, smoking) and detection bias are possible; the abstract does not state the RD denominator or whether effects differed by psoriasis severity or treatment.

Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology

Intralesional cemiplimab for patients with early-stage cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma: Results from a dose-escalation study with expansion cohorts

Migden M, Ibrahim SF, Strasswimmer J et al. · 2026 Oct 30
Study Type: Open-label, phase 1 dose-escalation study with two expansion cohorts (n=41; NCT03889912).
Key Question: Is low-dose intralesional cemiplimab safe and effective as a non-surgical treatment for early-stage (1-2 cm) cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma?
Key Findings:
  • Safety was acceptable; in the expansion cohorts, all treatment-emergent adverse events were grade ≤2.
  • Cohort A (5 mg weekly for 6 weeks): visual and pathologic complete response both 58.3% at Week 13.
  • Cohort B (5 mg every 2 weeks for 6 weeks): visual complete response 41.7%, pathologic complete response 66.7%. Cohort sizes appear to be around 12 each (inferred from percentages; not stated).
Clinical Relevance: If confirmed in larger trials, this could offer a systemic-sparing, non-surgical option for selected low-risk CSCC, relevant to NHS surgical capacity and patients unsuitable for surgery, though cemiplimab is not currently licensed for intralesional use.
Limitations: Very small, uncontrolled single-lesion study with potentially variable injection technique, so efficacy estimates are imprecise and no comparison with surgery or standard care is possible.

British Journal of Dermatology

HiSQOL-mini: Development and Validation of a Shortened Version of the Hidradenitis Suppurativa Quality of Life (HiSQOL) Instrument

Ingram JR, Espy J, Garg A et al. · 2026 Oct 21
Study Type: Instrument development and psychometric validation study (secondary analysis of THESEUS cohort and BE HEARD I/II phase 3 trial data, with patient-partner-led consensus workshops).
Key Question: Can the 17-item HiSQOL be shortened to a valid, reliable, responsive instrument suitable for routine clinical use in HS?
Key Findings:
  • HiSQOL-mini comprises four items (pain, feeling down or depressed, walking, getting dressed), selected via item-total correlations and two consensus workshops led by patient research partners. Scores range 0–16.
  • Reported validity, reliability and responsiveness were good (no coefficients given in the abstract).
  • Minimal important difference is a 3-point reduction; clinically meaningful change is a 5-point reduction. Severity bands: 0 none, 1–2 mild, 3–4 moderate, 5–6 severe, 7–16 very severe.
Clinical Relevance: A four-item, HISTORIC-aligned HS quality-of-life measure could make QoL assessment feasible in time-pressured NHS HS clinics and standardise outcome reporting in audit and research.
Limitations: Psychometric validation used the same trial dataset (BE HEARD) that informed item selection, with no independent validation cohort reported in the abstract.

Journal of Investigative Dermatology

Pathogenic Keratinocyte States and Fibroblast Niches Define the Tissue Microenvironment in Severe Hidradenitis Suppurativa

Du-Harpur X, Ganier C, Mazin P et al. · 2026 Oct 22
Study Type: Laboratory/translational study (single-cell RNA-sequencing and spatial transcriptomics of lesional skin from severe HS patients). Sample size not stated in abstract.
Key Question: How do keratinocyte, fibroblast and immune cell populations interact spatially within severe HS lesions to sustain disease?
Key Findings:
  • A migratory S100+ keratinocyte state was enriched in HS lesions.
  • Two spatially distinct fibroblast populations were identified: COL6A5+ papillary fibroblasts, co-localised with undifferentiated keratinocytes, and APOD+ fibroblasts, associated with immune-rich regions containing activated B cells and plasma cells, consistent with tertiary lymphoid organ (TLO)-like aggregates.
  • Ligand-receptor inference predicted extensive fibroblast-keratinocyte and fibroblast-immune signalling. These interactions are computational predictions, not experimentally validated.
Clinical Relevance: The findings propose a stromal-epithelial-immune niche model that may help explain the limited response of many patients to single-pathway biologics in severe HS, relevant to treatment-refractory cases in NHS biologic pathways.
Limitations: Findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, with predicted cell interactions lacking functional validation and no clinical outcome data.

Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology

Optimizing surgery in hidradenitis suppurativa

Vilarrasa E, Guillem P, Horváth B et al. · 2026 Oct 21
Study Type: Narrative review (evidence and expert consensus; no systematic methodology described in abstract).
Key Question: How can surgical management of hidradenitis suppurativa be optimised in terms of technique selection, timing, imaging, reconstruction, post-operative care and integration with medical therapy?
Key Findings:
  • Technique should match disease extent: deroofing for localised tunnels, STEEP for confluent tunnels, wide excision for extensive disease, each with characteristic recurrence rates (not quantified in abstract).
  • Operating on medically controlled tissue ("surgical window") and using pre-operative ultrasound (MRI for deep or anogenital disease) reduces incomplete excision and local complications.
  • Secondary intention healing remains standard for large defects; combining surgery with systemic therapy appears to improve response rates without a consistent increase in adverse events.
Clinical Relevance: Offers a framework for UK multidisciplinary HS pathways, supporting earlier, imaging-guided surgical referral alongside biologic therapy.
Limitations: As a narrative review, it lacks pooled quantitative data, and the abstract notes the supporting evidence is largely observational, with a need for higher-quality prospective research.

British Journal of Dermatology

Understanding the Experiences and Needs of Parents With Children With Epidermolysis Bullosa. A Qualitative Study to Inform the Development of a Self-help Toolkit

Hughes O, Martin F, Thompson AR · 2026 Oct 29
Study Type: Qualitative study (semi-structured interviews with thematic analysis); sample size not stated in the abstract.
Key Question: What are the psychosocial support needs of parents caring for children with epidermolysis bullosa (EB), and how might a self-help toolkit address them?
Key Findings:
  • Parents reported complex emotional burden, including sadness, worry, uncertainty about the future, and guilt.
  • Expert healthcare professionals' accounts corroborated parental experiences and endorsed the need for a tailored psychosocial self-help intervention.
  • Findings indicate any intervention should address wider family impact (including siblings) and the psychosocial cost of continuing care; acceptance and commitment therapy-based approaches may be suitable if adapted systemically.
Clinical Relevance: Supports integrating family-focused psychosocial provision into UK EB services, where parental caregiving burden is substantial and structured psychological support is not routinely available.
Limitations: The abstract does not report participant numbers, recruitment setting or sampling approach, so transferability is unclear, particularly for a rare condition with likely small, specialist-centre samples.
